vignette:
Amir works the late shift at a burger chain off the interstate. He always takes the drive-through station now, even though it pays the same as front counter. The drive-through speaker lets him face the wall, hands busy with bags and trays, eyes fixed on the cars rolling past his window. He tells his manager it’s because he likes the rhythm—but the truth is the counter faces the entire dining room, and that glass door slides open so easily.

A year ago, on a Tuesday night just like this one, Amir was wiping down the counter when three men walked in. He remembers noticing the way their jackets hung heavy. One of them pulled a silver revolver from his waistband and pointed it at the register girl, Christina, a nineteen-year-old college kid who always hummed while she worked. They were shouting. The gun went off. Amir didn’t see the bullet hit her—he had already dropped behind the counter, hands over his ears—but he heard her fall. He stayed frozen until the police came, smelling hot grease and something metallic.

Christina survived. The surgeon said the bullet missed her spine by two inches. Amir never visited her in the hospital. He couldn’t. He called in sick for three weeks after, lying on his studio sofa with the blinds closed, replaying the sound of that shot. When he finally went back, the manager had replaced the broken glass and put out new menus, as if it had never happened. Amir keeps his coat on during his shift now, even in summer, because the back of his neck feels exposed without it.

He doesn’t sleep well. Most nights he lies awake scanning the shadows in his apartment, listening for footsteps in the hallway. The buzzer from the kitchen timer makes him flinch. Car doors slamming outside his window make his hands go cold. He stopped taking the subway after a man in a puffy jacket got on near his stop—puffy jacket like one of the robbers wore. Now he walks the two miles home, even in the rain, because he can see people coming from farther away.

Amir has become quiet. His coworkers used to joke with him; now they just leave him alone. He doesn’t call his mother back home in Lebanon as often. She asks why his voice sounds tight. He says he’s just tired. He avoids any news story about a robbery, any movie with a gun. Last month he left a grocery store halfway through checkout because a kid in the next aisle popped a balloon and Amir’s heart started hammering so hard he thought he’d pass out.

Sometimes, right before falling asleep, he sees the muzzle of that gun again. He smells the burnt powder. He feels the cold tile biting into his knees. And he wonders why he didn’t do more—why he just curled up like a child instead of helping Christina. She’s fine now, but Amir is not. His body remembers that night more clearly than his mind does. It twitches, it sweats, it startles at nothing. The restaurant's fryer hisses like a warning, and every time the bell above the door rings, Amir’s stomach drops. He doesn’t look up. He just keeps his hands on the bags, keeps his back to the room, and waits for the sound to pass.
